# Claim Ledger — *The Governable Mind*, draft v2

Checked 2026-09-16 by two verification subagents (Part A: the 2025–2026 legal and policy record; Part B: the scholarly and philosophical apparatus), each against sources fetched and read in this session or against the editor's persisted source notes from round 1 where the v2 wording matches the round-1 fix. Claim IDs refer to the inventory in `00-piece-brief.md`. Line numbers refer to `drafts/v2.md`. The author's response letter's list of secondary-only claims (Heppner; the WIRED line; Zuboff; Boire; the nationality rationale) was checked first: three of the five are now pinned to primaries (Heppner's opinion; Anthropic's own July 1 post; Boire in reproduction), one is corroborated by seven independent quotations (Williams), and one must be de-quoted (the WIRED line).

## Summary (combined)
- Claims inventoried: 108 (T1: 44 · T2: 58 · T3: 6); every N item checked fresh; every R item's v2 wording confirmed against the round-1 fix (all round-1 fixes were applied)
- Checked fresh: 66 (Part A 41; Part B 25) — Verified: 41 · Substantially accurate: 19 · Misleading in context: 3 · Unsupported: 0 · Contradicted: 3 · Unverifiable: 0. Reuse confirmations: 42. Bibliographic checks: 37 references (two need correcting: [30] section pinpoint; [69] retitle; several to add primaries: [34], [36], [77]).
- Major-issue escalations (Tier 1 Contradicted or Misleading):
  1. **III16 / VII3 (l.84, l.152) — Contradicted.** The Maine warrant did not identify the suspect from his prompts; agents identified him by other means before OpenAI answered. The warrant *searched* by prompt.
  2. **VII3-scope (l.152) — Contradicted.** "The first documented instance" of an institution reconstructing deliberation from chatbot traces is not the September 2025 warrant: Las Vegas police read a bomber's ChatGPT planning queries to the press in January 2025; a Roanoke jury heard a Snapchat My AI exchange as premeditation evidence in October 2024. Only "first known federal warrant to OpenAI" holds.
  3. **VI5 / XII2 (l.260) — Contradicted in one clause.** H.R. 9917's shutdown order is not "reviewable in court within days": 48-hour petition to the Secretary (no stay), five-day agency decision, D.C. Circuit petition within 60 days, no deadline on the court. Also "the Secretary identifies" → "the provider or the Secretary identifies"; "throttle" is in the discretionary framework, not the mandatory list.
  4. **XIII2 (l.276) — Misleading in context.** "Do not support retries or appeals" is OpenAI's wording (altered from "does") attributed to the laboratories' tier generally; Anthropic's tier allows retries, has an appeal form, and says it expects "to occasionally decline eligible applications incorrectly."
  Tier 2 Misleading: V3 (l.122: Heppner had three independent grounds; "turned on" overstates; l.222's "turned partly on" is right).
- Reported against interest, in the draft's favour: X9 (Anthropic's own July 1 post supplies the nationality rationale the author thought secondary-only; "nineteen" and "eighteen" days are each right for their sentence); III19 (the Heppner opinion is reachable and confirms every quoted word and the device seizure); X5 (OpenAI's own post says it signed the Nvidia letter; the PDF has OpenAI and no Anthropic); X11 (Axios: the current framework "explicitly says nothing in it should be interpreted as restricting open models once they've been released"); XV1 (Williams p. 11, Unverifiable in round 1, now pinned by seven scholarly quotations); III9 (Baumgartner's diary is the evidence "on which the Government mainly relies"; Blitz's fn. 103 characterizes it exactly as the draft needs); III7 (Alegre states the absoluteness→duty inference at p. 225); VII6 (Cohen's own footnote cites Deleuze); III4 (Shaheed "relays, without adopting" is exact); III2 (GC22 never uses "forum internum").
- Other fixes: X10 (thirteen days, not "two weeks"); X11 (de-quote the WIRED line); III20 (the June 22 order quashed only the OpenAI warrant); XIII1 ("ordered produced"); P8 (same); II4 (Tesink et al. "noted," not "warned against"); X2 (OpenAI called the August revocations an error on its side); III15 (four and a half months); [30] §3.B not §3.A, and the Bublitz agreement is with a chapter forthcoming in vol. 2 (2026), not a 2021 publication.

### P7 · Tier 1 · Verified
> "an outside party, a safety nonprofit that found GLM-5.2 'refused none of the offensive-security or biological tasks' it was given while Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7 declined its offensive-cyber evaluations." (l.14)
- **Finding:** SaferAI, "GLM-5.2 Risk Evaluation Report," Aug. 2, 2026: "Beyond capability, it refused none of the offensive-security or biological tasks" (verbatim). On Opus 4.7: "Closed-weight frontier models are more likely to be gated by content filters such as Claude Opus 4.7 which declined our CyberGym evaluations and there is no option to self-serve and bypass the filters." Nothing in the report reverses the meaning; it also notes "no model refused a task on either LAB-Bench or BioMysteryBench," i.e., the bio-refusal asymmetry is not unique to GLM-5.2, which the draft does not claim.
- **Evidence:** [SaferAI, GLM-5.2 Risk Evaluation Report, Aug. 2, 2026](https://www.safer-ai.org/research/glm-5-2-evaluation-report); [TechCrunch, Aug. 4, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/04/open-weight-ai-models-are-catching-up-to-the-frontier-the-safety-gap-remains/) (reused note: techcrunch-open-weight-safety-gap-saferai-2026).

### III14 · Tier 1 · Verified
> "*Chatrie*, decided on June 29, 2026, held the same of a location history acquired from Google, the Court adding that it does not matter 'that the materials obtained were handed over by a third-party tech company.'" CRS: federal courts "have not yet had the occasion to determine" … "or whether that expectation is forfeited by virtue of the third-party doctrine." (l.80)
- **Finding:** Slip opinion, No. 25–112, argued April 27, decided June 29, 2026, slip op. at 29 (PDF p. 34, running head "29 Cite as: 609 U. S. ____ (2026)"): "For all those reasons, we hold that police officers invade a cell-phone user's reasonable expectation of privacy when they access his Location History. It does not matter if the time period scrutinized was only two hours. Nor does it matter that the materials obtained were handed over by a third-party tech company." The draft's fragment is verbatim and the context does not qualify it. CRS LSB11429 (May 5, 2026), p. 3: "It appears that federal courts have not yet had the occasion to determine whether a user maintains a reasonable expectation of privacy in chatbot histories, or whether that expectation is forfeited by virtue of the third-party doctrine." Verbatim. "For fifty years" is fair for *Miller* (1976)/*Smith* (1979).
- **Evidence:** [Chatrie v. United States, slip op. (PDF)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-112_0am4.pdf) — downloaded and text-extracted; [CRS LSB11429 (PDF)](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/LSB/PDF/LSB11429/LSB11429.1.pdf) (reused note: crs-lsb11429-ai-fourth-amendment; venable-chatrie-jul-2026 for the 6–3/Kagan detail).
- **Fix:** none. Ref [32] docket and page are correct.

### III15 · Tier 1 · Verified
> ordered OpenAI in May 2025 "to preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted," so that for four months no consumer's deletion of a conversation took effect, and in January 2026 the district judge affirmed the production of twenty million de-identified conversations, reasoning that the privacy interest in conversations "which users voluntarily disclosed to OpenAI" is weaker than the interest in a wiretapped call. (l.84)
- **Finding:** Order of May 13, 2025 (Wang, M.J.), 25-md-3143: "OpenAI is NOW DIRECTED to preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted on a going forward basis," whether deletion would occur "at a user's request or because of 'numerous privacy laws and regulations.'" Order of Jan. 5, 2026 (Stein, J.), p. 3: the logs are conversations "users voluntarily disclosed to OpenAI and which OpenAI retains in the normal course of its business"; "privacy interests in the wiretapped recordings of private phone conversations in *Rajaratnam* are stronger than the privacy interests in users' conversations with ChatGPT"; p. 4: "OpenAI's objections are denied and Judge Wang's orders are affirmed." The draft's quotation and paraphrase are exact; ref [34] "at 3" is correct.
- **Evidence:** [Preservation order, May 13, 2025 (PDF)](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/NYT-v-OpenAI-Preservation-Order-5-13-25.pdf); [Stein order, Jan. 5, 2026 (PDF)](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/NYT-v-OpenAI-Order-1-5-26.pdf); (reused notes: engadget-openai-preservation-order-lifted; nyt-v-openai-preservation-order; natlawreview-openai-20m-logs-jan-2026).

### III16 · Tier 1 · Contradicted (major escalation)
> "In September 2025 the first known federal warrant to OpenAI identified a suspect, known to investigators only by a username, from the content of two prompts he had described." (l.84); "the warrant of September 2025 that found a man from two prompts, because the questions he had asked were the most identifying thing about him." (l.152)
- **Finding:** Three things are right: it was the first known federal warrant to OpenAI for user data (Forbes; Pfefferkorn); investigators "had been unable to identify the suspect beyond an online username" (CRS p. 3); the warrant was built on "two unique, specific prompts" the suspect had described to an undercover HSI agent (CRS pp. 3–4; Forbes: "What would happen if Sherlock Holmes met Q from Star Trek?" and a 200,000-word-poem request). What is wrong is the verb. Forbes, which read the unsealed file: the government did not need OpenAI's data to identify him; he had told the undercover agent about health assessments, seven years in Germany, and his father's service in Afghanistan, and military records identified 36-year-old Drew Hoehner, who had worked at Ramstein Air Force Base; OpenAI's return was "one Excel spreadsheet." Cybersecurity News, relaying Forbes: "Ironically, the OpenAI data proved unnecessary for identification." So the warrant *searched* for the account behind two prompts (the cognitive-legibility point survives: the prompts were the only searchable handle); it did not identify or "find" the man. Gizmodo's reading ("the government already believes it has identified the criminal") agrees on the outcome. The unsealing was mid-October 2025; CRS dates the warrant to September.
- **Evidence:** [Forbes (Brewster), Oct. 20, 2025, via Law Report Group reprint (PDF)](https://cdn.lawreportgroup.com/acuris/files/Law-Report-Group-Files-New/AI%20Warrants%20Pt%201%20Forbes%20article.pdf); [Cybersecurity News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/dhs-warrant-openai/); [Gizmodo (Ropek), Oct. 20, 2025](https://gizmodo.com/dhs-asks-openai-to-unmask-user-behind-chatgpt-prompts-possibly-the-first-such-case-2000674472); [CRS LSB11429](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/LSB/PDF/LSB11429/LSB11429.1.pdf), pp. 3–4; [Pfefferkorn, Oct. 24, 2025](https://cyberlaw.stanford.edu/blog/2025/10/eight-or-so-questions-to-ask-about-the-chatgpt-warrant/) (reused note: pfefferkorn-eight-questions-chatgpt-warrant).
- **Fix:** l.84: "In September 2025 the first known federal warrant to OpenAI sought the account behind two prompts a suspect, known to investigators only by a username, had described to an undercover agent; by the time OpenAI answered, agents had identified him by other means." l.152: "the warrant of September 2025 that searched for a man by two prompts, because the questions he had asked were the most identifying thing investigators could put to the provider." The essay's point (the prompt as identifier) is stronger stated this way, because it does not depend on the return.

### VII3-scope · Tier 1 · Contradicted (major escalation)
> "The first documented instance is already on the record: the warrant of September 2025 …" (l.152)
- **Finding:** (a) Pfefferkorn's and Forbes's claim is the narrow one, "the first known federal search warrant asking OpenAI for user data," and it holds. The draft's claim is the broad one, the first documented instance of an institution reconstructing deliberation from chatbot traces, and it does not. (b) Las Vegas: on Jan. 7, 2025 the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department described, at a press conference, Matthew Livelsberger's ChatGPT queries before the Jan. 1 Cybertruck explosion. NBC (Winter, Blankstein, Planas, Jan. 7, 2025): he "queried ChatGPT for information about how he could put together an explosive, how fast a round would need to be fired for the explosives found in the truck to go off — not just catch fire — and what laws he would need to get around to get the materials"; Sheriff McMahill: "I think this is the first incident that I'm aware of on U.S. soil where ChatGPT is utilized to help an individual build a particular device." KMPH (Jan. 7, 2025): "A search of his digital records found that he entered several queries on ChatGPT," including Tannerite purchase limits in Colorado, whether a gun could detonate it, and the largest gun store in Denver. ABC (Jan. 7, 2025) independently reports the same briefing. Fox5 (Nov. 3, 2025), on the 78-page police report: officials "were able to recover Livelsberger's manifesto, internet search history, social media activity, encrypted emails, notes, and his ChatGPT history." The sources I opened say the history was recovered from his records; none says OpenAI was served. (c) Earlier still: Roanoke Times (Hammack, Oct. 20, 2024): "A search warrant for the defendant's cellphone led to the recovery of a lengthy chat" with Snapchat's My AI on the night of a July 10, 2022 killing ("I'm about to fight"; "What if I shot them if they step on my property with hostile intent?"), which prosecutors argued showed the defendant "acted with premeditation." CNN (Levenson, May 2, 2026) lists further device-recovered chatbot evidence (Palisades, Oct. 2025; USF killings, Apr. 2026). (d) Palisades timing: the "cigarettes" question was typed Jan. 1, 2025 and recovered from the defendant's iPhone; the charging document is dated Oct. 8, 2025, after the Maine warrant was issued (Sept. 2025, per CRS) and before it was reported (Oct. 20). So the Maine warrant is the first documented instance of the *provider* being made to search its records by prompt; device-recovered chatbot histories had been institutional evidence of deliberation since at least October 2024, and publicly since January 2025.
- **Evidence:** [NBC News, Jan. 7, 2025](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/driver-las-vegas-cybertruck-explosion-used-chatgpt-plan-blast-authorit-rcna186704); [ABC News, Jan. 7, 2025](https://abcnews.com/US/las-vegas-cybertruck-explosion-suspect-chatgpt-plan-attack/story?id=117428523); [KMPH, Jan. 7, 2025](https://kmph.com/news/nation-world/las-vegas-police-new-update-cybertruck-explosion-investigation-matthew-livelsberger-lvmpd-fbi-atf-trump-international-hotel-crime-colorado-nevada); [Fox5 Vegas, Nov. 3, 2025](https://www.fox5vegas.com/2025/11/03/report-details-police-investigation-into-cybertruck-explosion-trump-international-hotel-las-vegas/); [Roanoke Times, Oct. 20, 2024](https://roanoke.com/news/local/crime-courts/roanoke-teen-convicted-of-murder-consulted-ai-chatbot/article_a49c68ae-8d7e-11ef-b321-d3bb74ec3649.html); [CNN via KRDO, May 2, 2026](https://krdo.com/news/2026/05/02/how-chatgpt-conversations-became-a-treasure-trove-of-evidence-in-criminal-investigations/); Forbes and CRS as in III16.
- **Fix:** l.152: "The first documented instance of the provider being made to search is already on the record: the warrant of September 2025 …" and, if the essay wants the fuller record, one clause: "device-recovered chatbot histories had been evidence of intent since 2024, and the Las Vegas police read a bomber's planning questions to the press in January 2025." The Las Vegas case is also the better illustration of the §VII definition (reconstruction, classification, inference from traces) because the reconstruction was done and announced.

### III17 · Tier 1 · Verified
> "a hypothetical put to ChatGPT, whether one is at fault if a fire is lit by one's cigarettes, has been quoted in an arson charging document as evidence of state of mind." (l.84)
- **Finding:** Criminal complaint affidavit (ATF special agent), *United States v. Rinderknecht* (C.D. Cal.), Oct. 8, 2025, ¶26: "During the call, RINDERKNECHT typed a question into the ChatGPT app on his iPhone, asking, 'Are you at fault if a fire is lift [sic] because of your cigarettes.'" ¶37(c): the question "indicates that RINDERKNECHT wanted to preserve evidence of himself trying to assist in the suppression of the fire and he wanted to create evidence regarding a more innocent explanation for the cause of the fire." CRS p. 2 quotes the same line from "charging documents." The paraphrase is fair; "as evidence of state of mind" is a fair description of a consciousness-of-guilt inference. The question was recovered from the defendant's own iPhone (a screen recording), not from OpenAI, which the draft does not claim otherwise. The case is pending (indicted; defense has moved to exclude ChatGPT evidence per CNN), which the draft's "charging document" wording respects.
- **Evidence:** [Criminal complaint, redacted (PDF, Fox News mirror)](https://static.foxnews.com/foxnews.com/content/uploads/2025/10/palisades-fire-criminal-complaint_redacted.pdf); [DOJ case page](https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/united-states-v-jonathan-rinderknecht) (not opened; located by search); [CRS LSB11429](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/LSB/PDF/LSB11429/LSB11429.1.pdf), p. 2.
- **Fix:** none.

### III18 · Tier 1 · Verified
> conversations indicating a plan to harm others are routed to human reviewers who "may refer" an imminent threat to law enforcement, while self-harm cases are not referred, "to respect people's privacy given the uniquely private nature of ChatGPT interactions." (l.84)
- **Finding:** OpenAI, "Helping people when they need it most": "When we detect users who are planning to harm others, we route their conversations to specialized pipelines where they are reviewed by a small team … authorized to take action, including banning accounts. If human reviewers determine that a case involves an imminent threat of serious physical harm to others, we may refer it to law enforcement." "We are currently not referring self-harm cases to law enforcement to respect people's privacy given the uniquely private nature of ChatGPT interactions." Both fragments verbatim. The page shows no date; Aug. 26, 2025 is the date carried by contemporaneous coverage (reused note dates coverage Aug. 31).
- **Evidence:** [OpenAI, "Helping people when they need it most"](https://openai.com/index/helping-people-when-they-need-it-most/) (via reader proxy); (reused note: slashdot-openai-scanning-referral-aug-2025).
- **Fix:** none.

### III19 · Tier 1 · Verified (primary reached)
> "a federal judge held that a defendant's exchanges with Claude, prepared to brief his lawyers, were not privileged: 'Because Claude is not an attorney, that alone disposes' of the claim, and confidentiality failed in any case because the provider's terms let it retain, train on, and disclose them." (l.84); ref [36] "820 F. Supp. 3d 292 … slip op. at 5–6, as quoted in" the HLR Blog.
- **Finding:** Memorandum, *United States v. Heppner*, No. 25-cr-00503 (JSR), Dkt. 27 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 17, 2026), following a bench ruling of Feb. 10. Pages 5–6: "Because Claude is not an attorney, see ECF No. 23-6, that alone disposes of Heppner's claim of privilege." Three independent grounds: Claude is not an attorney; no confidentiality; the communications were not for the purpose of obtaining legal advice. On confidentiality (pp. 6–7): Anthropic's privacy policy "collects data on both users' 'inputs' and Claude's 'outputs,' that it uses such data to 'train' Claude, and that Anthropic reserves the right to disclose such data to a host of 'third parties,' including 'governmental regulatory authorities'"; hence "Heppner could have had no 'reasonable expectation of confidentiality in his communications' with Claude."
